articles.title: Steve Ballmer built a $164 billion fortune; his philanthropy is shifting towards locally led foundations tackling poverty and expanding education, including a preschool initiative worth up to $1.7 billion
articles.summary: Steve Ballmer, the former Microsoft chief executive whose fortune is estimated at $164 billion by Forbes, is changing how his family directs its
articles.body: Steve Ballmer, the former Microsoft chief executive whose fortune is estimated at $164 billion by Forbes, is changing how his family directs its philanthropic resources. Rather than continuing to distribute money across a broad range of grants, Ballmer and his wife, Connie Ballmer, are moving towards a strategy that combines locally led organisations with large-scale initiatives aimed at improving economic mobility. Their approach focuses on helping children and families overcome poverty through education, early learning and other support systems. The shift includes the creation of three independent regional philanthropic organisations and a commitment of up to $1.7 billion to expand preschool access in Washington state over a decade.How Steve Ballmer built his fortune at MicrosoftBallmer joined Microsoft in 1980 as its 30th employee after leaving Stanford University's business school. He rose through the company's leadership ranks, becoming president in 1998 and chief executive in 2000, succeeding co-founder Bill Gates. He led the technology company until 2014.Much of Ballmer's wealth comes from his Microsoft shareholding. Forbes reported that he retained most of his stock after retiring and remained the company's largest individual shareholder. His wealth has therefore continued to be influenced by changes in Microsoft's market value. He also purchased the NBA's Los Angeles Clippers in 2014 for $2 billion.Forbes estimated Ballmer's net worth at $164 billion on October 29, 2026. Bloomberg's Billionaires Index gave a higher estimate of $186 billion, reflecting differences in the organisations' valuation methods. These figures are estimates that can change with market prices, rather than fixed measures of his wealth.Why the Ballmers are changing their philanthropic approachSteve and Connie Ballmer established Ballmer Group in 2015 to support efforts that improve economic mobility for children and families in the United States. Its work has included school readiness, job training, safer communities and programmes intended to help children thrive.In an October 2026 statement explaining the strategy, Ballmer Group said it wanted to direct more resources towards initiatives capable of reaching large numbers of people. Instead of expanding its team and increasing the number of grants it makes, the organisation plans to concentrate on fewer, larger initiatives, organisations and networks.The change reflects a shift in how the couple wants their money to be deployed, rather than an abandonment of their existing mission. The group said its experience working with different organisations had helped it identify opportunities to use established systems and partnerships to deliver support at greater scale. The strategy also means it will step back from annual grants to some organisations it has supported in previous years.Three independent philanthropies to focus on local needsIn July 2026, Steve and Connie Ballmer announced plans to establish three independent philanthropic organisations in Southeast Michigan, Los Angeles County and Washington state. Named MoveUp Southeast Michigan, MoveUp LA and MoveUp Washington, they are intended to continue the Ballmers' regional work while placing decision-making closer to the communities being served.The organisations will operate independently from Ballmer Group but will continue to receive funding from the Ballmers. Each will have its own board and will build on existing work to improve economic mobility for children and families.The couple said the organisations were intended to become long-term resources in their respective regions. Existing regional teams will transition to the new organisations, and the Ballmers said current grant commitments would continue during the transition.The structure is designed to give local leaders greater flexibility to respond to community needs, maintain relationships with organisations and support work over multiple years. Ballmer Group, meanwhile, intends to concentrate its national efforts on a smaller number of initiatives that can operate at a larger scale.Inside the $1.7 billion preschool initiativeOne of the clearest examples of the Ballmers' new approach is their commitment of up to $1.7 billion over 10 years to expand access to preschool in Washington state.The funding is intended to support up to 10,000 additional preschool places annually through the state's Early Childhood Education and Assistance Program, known as ECEAP. The programme provides early learning opportunities for eligible children, particularly those from families facing financial and other barriers.Rather than establishing a separate preschool system, the Ballmers are building on an existing public programme. Their contribution is intended to help Washington expand access to early education while using the state's established infrastructure and provider network.The commitment is conditional on the state maintaining its existing funding for the programme. The $1.7 billion figure represents the maximum planned investment over the decade, not money already spent or a single payment made upfront. The initiative is an example of how the Ballmers intend to use large commitments and established systems to reach more children.Beyond preschool: summer learning and affordable housingThe Ballmers' strategy extends beyond early childhood education. Another initiative, DiscoverWorks, supports summer learning programmes through partnerships with school districts, charter schools and community-based organisations. The programmes combine academic learning with enrichment activities to help children remain engaged outside the school year.Ballmer Group said it had invested more than $280 million in DiscoverWorks during its first three years, reaching nearly 110,000 students. The organisation has indicated that it wants to expand the initiative as demand grows.Affordable housing is another part of its work. Through the Washington Family Housing Fund, Ballmer Group provides zero-interest, forgivable loans of up to $150,000 per housing unit to encourage developers to build homes that remain affordable for at least 60 years. Its stated goal is to invest up to $1.5 billion to support the creation of 10,000 homes across Washington.A focus on scale and long-term impactThe Ballmers' evolving strategy brings together two approaches to philanthropy. Their regional organisations are intended to preserve local relationships and give community-based leaders greater control over funding decisions. Their national initiatives, meanwhile, will focus on large-scale programmes that can use existing systems to reach more children and families.The approach also involves difficult choices. Ballmer Group has acknowledged that concentrating resources on fewer, larger initiatives will mean stepping back from some annual grants, even to organisations whose work it values.The broader objective remains improving economic mobility for children and families in the United States. By combining locally led philanthropy with substantial investments in preschool, summer learning and affordable housing, the Ballmers are seeking to direct more of their resources towards programmes they believe can produce lasting results. Whether the approach achieves that ambition will depend on how effectively these organisations and initiatives deliver support over time.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: The political obituary can wait: Lula, Bibi and the art of survival
articles.summary: One is a Left-wing icon challenging Trump's dominance of Latin America.
articles.body: One is a Left-wing icon challenging Trump's dominance of Latin America. The other is a Right-wing nationalist who helped persuade the US president to attack Iran. Yet, despite their ideological differences, Lula and Netanyahu have shown why writing political obituaries can be a dangerous business.Opposite poles, one instinctThey could hardly be further apart. Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, 80, leads Latin America's biggest left-wing party. Benjamin Netanyahu, 77, heads the most right-wing government in Israel's history and is Donald Trump's closest ally abroad. One has spent the year denouncing American power in his hemisphere. The other spent it pulling American power into his.Yet within a span of three days, both did what their critics thought they could not. Lula came from behind to win a fourth term on October 25. Two days later, Netanyahu turned an election night that the exit polls called a rout into something closer to a draw.Both have given master classes in the oldest skill in politics: Staying alive.Interestingly, US President Donald Trump had a stake in both contests. He openly endorsed Netanyahu, and he has long counted the Bolsonaro family as friends. His scoreline is 1-1.Lula: The comeback that stalled the Donroe DoctrineBrazil's first round on October 4 looked like the end. Flavio Bolsonaro, senator and eldest son of the jailed former president, took about 47% of the valid vote to Lula's 45%, defying final polls that had the president ahead. Lula admitted he had expected to win outright. The first survey afterwards gave Bolsonaro a six-point runoff lead.Three weeks later, the official count gave Lula 51.79% to 48.21%. The result halted a right-wing wave that had already delivered victories for Jose Antonio Kast in Chile, Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia and Keiko Fujimori in Peru.How did he do it? Lula went back to the streets and went after the Bolsonaro family directly, raising its alleged links to militias. Flávio had greeted his first-round lead by proclaiming the end of the Workers' Party era. It proved premature.Trump's "Donroe Doctrine", his muscular update of the Monroe Doctrine, has split the hemisphere into friends and foes since the US seized Nicolas Maduro in January. Brazil was its biggest prize. Flavio had promised to join the US-backed Americas Shield security pact and to free his father. Lula has halted the Trump wagon. He is now the most powerful leftist still standing in Washington's way.The defeat has since turned into a spectacle. Flavio crossed into Argentina before flying to Miami with his family, after Trump offered them a way out. From the United States, he now casts himself as a victim of political persecution. Lula, meanwhile, is pressing ahead with his agenda.Netanyahu: Written off, not counted outIn Israel, the script ran the other way. Almost every pre-election poll put Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc in front. When voting closed on October 27, the broadcasters' exit polls showed Eisenkot ahead by two or three seats, and his supporters partied in Tel Aviv.The count told another story. With about 90% of ballots tallied, Likud is the largest party with 26 seats, and Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc holds 53 seats to Eisenkot's 48.Turnout hit a historic high. Arab Israelis voted in record numbers, while Netanyahu's own base came out to defend him. Likud's response was telling: It accused the Arab parties of stealing the election. Trump, for his part, claimed his endorsement had turned the tide and hailed a come-from-behind performance.Let’s be clear: This is not an outright victory for Netanyahu. His bloc is eight seats short of a majority and down from 68 in the outgoing Knesset. But the opposition's arithmetic is worse. Arab parties won a record 19 seats, enough to give the anti-Netanyahu camp a majority, yet every Zionist opposition party except the Democrats has ruled out relying on them.Roughly 450,000 absentee ballots remain, official results are due on November 4, and coalition talks could drag on for months. If they fail, a unity government or yet another election both leave Netanyahu in office. Until then he stays on as caretaker, with full war powers, as a renewed war with Iran looms.Netanyahu is already playing for time. He has assured his far-right partners. President Isaac Herzog has urged the parties to avoid another election and keep an open mind, while Washington says it has not decided whether to weigh in.What survivors shareThe two leaders from the opposite spectrum share a toolkit. Both have come back from the dead before: Lula from 580 days in prison, Netanyahu from defeats in 1999 and 2021 and a corruption trial that has shadowed him since 2020. Both turned Trump into fuel. Lula wrapped himself in sovereignty against American tariffs and threats; Netanyahu wore Trump's endorsement, which the US president now claims turned the tide.Both also owe something to opponents who could not close the deal. Flavio Bolsonaro let a two-point lead slip away in three weeks. Eisenkot's camp has an anti-Netanyahu majority in the new Knesset but no agreed way to use it.The art of survivalThe twin results say something about the moment. Voters on both continents are angry, yet anger has not produced clean breaks. Leaders with deep networks and long memories still know how to bring their people to the polls, and how to make rivals pay for hesitation.Lula's fight is over; he will be sworn in on January 1, 2027. Netanyahu's is not, and he may yet lose the coalition game. But no one should hurry to write his political obituary.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: US intelligence confirms image shows China's secret spaceplane in orbit; design resembles X-37B
articles.summary: The US Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) has confirmed that a satellite image released in a newly declassified report shows China's experimental reusable
articles.body: The US Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) has confirmed that a satellite image released in a newly declassified report shows China's experimental reusable spaceplane in orbit, offering a clearer view of a spacecraft whose design closely resembles the US Space Force's X-37B.The higher-resolution image, captured by a satellite operated by Maxar Technologies, now known as Vantor, was included in the DIA's latest unclassified assessment of security challenges in space, released on October 26. Although a lower-resolution version had circulated publicly since 2024, the spacecraft's identity had not been confirmed at the time.The image shows a compact, shuttle-like vehicle with wings, twin vertical tails, an open payload bay and a rear-mounted module with solar panels deployed on either side. Its overall configuration resembles the X-37B, an uncrewed reusable spaceplane operated by the US Space Force, although the Chinese vehicle appears to have longer wings.“A key capability for reusable space activities are spaceplanes like this PRC [People’s Republic of China] Spaceplane captured by Maxar. Spaceplanes can launch into orbit to place objects in space or even test them and return to earth [sic],” reads the caption to the picture in DIA’s report.The exact date and circumstances of the satellite's observation have not been publicly disclosed in the DIA report. However, the image carries a 2024 copyright date, placing it within the period when China's spacecraft was conducting its third orbital mission.China has conducted four spaceplane missions since 2020China is understood to have conducted four orbital missions using its experimental reusable spaceplane since 2020. The latest mission began on February 7, 2026, and the spacecraft remained in orbit as of the latest available reports.The vehicle's activities have attracted attention because it has reportedly released smaller objects into orbit and carried out operations involving other spacecraft. During its third mission, which lasted from December 14, 2023, to September 6, 2024, the spaceplane was observed releasing multiple smaller objects. Their identities and purposes remain unknown.Analysis of open-source orbital tracking data by astrophysicist Jonathan McDowell also indicated that the spacecraft involved in the latest mission released and subsequently recaptured a smaller object during a series of orbital operations. These activities point to its ability to interact with objects in space, although its precise mission objectives remain undisclosed.The spacecraft is commonly referred to as Shenlong in Western reports, but its official designation and the model shown in the image have not been definitively established.The DIA report states that “China has two primary spaceplane models: the Shenlong and Tengyun,” without specifying which one appears in the photograph.China's Shenlong programme has been discussed publicly since at least 2007, when images emerged of what was believed to be a prototype or test vehicle mounted beneath an H-6 bomber. Separately, the state-run China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation unveiled its Tengyun reusable spaceplane concept in 2016. The proposed system was designed around a two-stage-to-orbit approach involving a carrier aircraft, rather than relying entirely on a conventional rocket launch.It remains unclear whether the planned Tengyun test targeted for 2025 took place.How China's spaceplane compares with the US X-37BThe Chinese vehicle shares several visible design features with the US Space Force's X-37B, including a winged body, payload bay and a configuration intended to support a return to Earth. Both spacecraft are uncrewed and designed for reusable orbital operations.The US has built two X-37B vehicles, which have flown a total of eight orbital missions since 2010. The spacecraft can carry experiments and payloads into orbit before returning to Earth for recovery and refurbishment. Much of its operational activity remains classified.China's spaceplane is also understood to launch aboard a conventional rocket before operating in orbit and returning to Earth for a runway landing. A secretive Chinese airbase in the country's northwest, featuring an exceptionally long runway, has been identified in reporting as a possible landing site for the vehicle, although the full details of its recovery operations remain unclear.The image does not establish whether the Chinese spacecraft carries weapons or is being used for offensive missions. However, its ability to manoeuvre, deploy objects and potentially interact with other spacecraft has raised questions about the military applications of reusable spaceplanes.DIA warns of growing competition in spaceThe DIA's report places reusable spaceplanes within a wider assessment of expanding space capabilities and the potential risks they pose to US and allied assets.In general, “spaceplanes are … reusable and feature enhanced maneuverability, making them more suitable for certain missions than traditional satellites,” DIA’s report notes.Such vehicles can potentially deploy small satellites, conduct experiments, inspect other spacecraft and return payloads to Earth. Their ability to alter trajectories and approach other objects also makes them useful for missions that conventional satellites may find more difficult to perform.The report also discusses China's development of counterspace capabilities, including ground-based laser weapons that could disrupt, degrade or damage satellites in low Earth orbit.“China has multiple ground-based laser weapons with varying power levels to disrupt, degrade, or damage satellites in LEO,” the DIA said. “By the late 2020s, China may field space-based directed energy systems and higher-powered ground-based directed energy systems capable of threatening satellites in higher orbits.”The assessment also points to China's testing of ground-based anti-satellite missiles, satellite servicing and refuelling technologies, and robotic systems that could potentially interact with spacecraft in orbit.China has expanded its space-based intelligence and surveillance capabilities in recent years, while the United States and Russia are also developing systems that can manoeuvre close to other satellites. Such activities have raised concerns about the potential for interference with, or attacks on, space assets.The DIA report also explains the economic rationale behind reusable technology, noting that conventional space access has relied heavily on expendable launch vehicles and spacecraft.“In general, access to space traditionally requires expendable spacecraft: single-use launch vehicles, satellites, and one-time use capsules designed to maximize performance. Reliance on expendable vehicles has made access to space expensive and exclusive,” DIA’s report explains. “Reusable technologies, while even more difficult and expensive to develop and build, stand to greatly reduce the cost of spaceflight by recovering, refurbishing, and reusing rocket stages, fairings, and capsules.”The newly released image provides a clearer look at China's experimental spaceplane, but its full capabilities, payloads and intended military role remain unknown. Its resemblance to the X-37B, combined with reported orbital manoeuvres and object deployments, underscores the growing role of reusable spacecraft in the increasingly competitive space domain.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Arunachal Pradesh chief minister Pema Khandu on Thursday said transgressions along the India-China border were not new, asserting that the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Arunachal Pradesh chief minister Pema Khandu on Thursday said transgressions along the India-China border were not new, asserting that the situation in the state’s border areas remained normal and that Indian armed forces were guarding the frontier effectively."Transgression has happened, no doubt. But it keeps happening; it is not a new thing," news agency PTI reported him as saying. Khandu added that the border was not clearly demarcated.Responding to questions about recent remarks on confrontations between Indian and Chinese troops at several locations along the Arunachal Pradesh border, Khandu said China did not recognise the McMahon Line, which separates Arunachal Pradesh from Tibet."Arunachal shares a very long border with Tibet-China, nearly 1,200 km. So, patrolling parties from their side sometimes cross over to our side. It's a transgression, not an intrusion," he said, without specifying the incidents he was referring to.Last week, Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director General Shatrujeet Kapur had said confrontations with Chinese troops continued at several locations along the border in Arunachal Pradesh, triggering a controversy.Khandu said he had come across the issue in news reports and described the matter as one that was being widely discussed."The media has unnecessarily ratcheted it up. The situation right now is normal, and our armed forces are guarding the border very well. There is no matter of tension right now," he said.Khandu was speaking ahead of the inauguration of the 14th International Tourism Mart in Tawang, attended by Union Tourism Minister Gajendra Singh Shekhawat and other dignitaries.Shekhawat said India’s borders were secure under the Narendra Modi government and there was no cause for concern. He also alleged that attempts were being made to create a false narrative around the issue.In August 2005, the Ministry of External Affairs had informed the Rajya Sabha that China disputed the legality of the McMahon Line dividing Arunachal Pradesh and the Tibet Autonomous Region.The ministry had also said that India and China had differing perceptions of the Line of Actual Control (LAC), with both sides conducting patrols in border areas and instances of transgression by Chinese military personnel occurring from time to time.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Jamia Millia Islamia has set May 15, 2027, as the deadline for approving and implementing its students’ union constitution and decided to revoke disciplinary action against protesting students. The university has also decided to hold students’ union elections within six weeks of the commencement of the next academic session, addressing three key demands raised by students during their 18-day protest seeking the restoration of the elected union, which has remained defunct since 2006.A student said the university had accepted all three demands, including a fixed deadline for implementing the constitution, an election schedule and the withdrawal of disciplinary proceedings against protesters.“Order has come in, it covers 3 points: 1) The approval and implementation of the Jamia Millia Islamia Students’ Union Constitution shall be completed by 15th May, 2027. We had demanded a date and they have announced a date, 2) The elections shall be conducted within 6 weeks of the start of the academic session, that is approximately within 6 weeks from 16 July 2027, 3) All disciplinary actions (taken against protesting students) will be revoked. They have accepted all 3 of our demands...We are calling off our hunger strike and protest...”The decision comes amid mounting tensions on campus over the demand for the restoration of the Jamia Millia Islamia Students’ Union (JMISU). Students had continued their agitation despite an earlier university order stating that elections would be held within 15 days of the approval of the union’s constitution. They had questioned the absence of a deadline for approving the constitution.The administration had also initiated disciplinary proceedings against students during the agitation. On October 27, the provost of Begum Hazrat Mahal Girls’ Hostel issued a show-cause notice to a student for allegedly obtaining emergency leave on misleading grounds and participating in the protest. The student was asked to submit a written explanation within 24 hours.The university has extended online classes until November 24 and shifted odd-semester examinations to online mode, citing the prevailing campus situation and concerns over students’ safety and security.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump says won’t ‘take sides’ in Brazil election, but calls it a ‘disgrace’
articles.summary: Comments come after Trump ally Flavio Bolsonaro fled to Miami in US and claimed, without evidence, that vote was stolen.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump declined to say if he agreed with the outcome of Sunday’s presidential elections in Brazil , but said he thought the contest was a “disgrace”.

“I thought the election was a great embarrassment to the people of Brazil,” Trump said in response to a question from a reporter on Thursday morning. “I watched the election. I didn’t take sides. I let it be. I was asked not to take sides by the president, the current president,” he said. “But when I watched what went down in Brazil, it was a disgrace…take a look at the market, I mean their market went down through the floor.”

Trump’s remarks came a day after former Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro and his family fled Brazil and landed in Miami, Florida, in the US on Wednesday.

Bolsonaro and his family were aided in their journey out of Brazil by Trump and his administration, the New York Times reported Thursday. Officials told the newspaper that the US government would likely provide the Bolsonaro family permanent residency.

On Sunday, Bolsonaro had lost a run-off election for Brazil’s president to the left-wing incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva by more than four million votes. The Brazilian real dropped against the dollar by 12 percent in spot trading after the election.

Brazil‘s Supreme Court had ordered Bolsonaro to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports shortly after the election, in an attempt to make sure the right-wing senator did not flee the country before he could be investigated for embezzlement and money laundering.

Bolsonaro left Brazil under cover of darkness, crossing by land with his wife and two daughters into Argentina, where the government of Trump’s right-wing ally President Javier Milei had granted them visas. The family then took a small private plane to Ecuador and later on to Miami, where they landed on Wednesday morning.

Shortly after landing, Bolsonaro issued a statement saying he was “the true elected president of Brazil” and the allegations against him were “a politically motivated witch-hunt”. He asked the international community “not to normalise what is happening in Brazil” and said he would lead the country’s opposition from the US. He did not provide evidence supporting his claims.

Bolsonaro’s own Liberal Party said on Monday that it was accepting the outcome of the election.

Although Brazil and the US have had an extradition treaty for several decades, it is unclear if Washington would turn over Bolsonaro, or whether Brazilian authorities would actually indict him and ask for such a move. On Wednesday, Brazil’s Supreme Court dispelled rumours that a search warrant had been issued for his home.

Flavio’s father, Brazil’s former President Jair Bolsonaro, undertook a very similar journey to Florida after he lost his bid for re-election in 2022. While he was in the US, the elder Bolsonaro’s supporters attempted to orchestrate a coup. Some in Brazil had called for the country to seek his extradition from the US. He later returned to Brazil and is currently under house arrest there.

articles.title: Cornell begins no confidence vote over handling of alleged gang rape
articles.summary: Faculty vote will continue until next Friday and could send message that school’s president has lost their confidence.
articles.body:
Cornell University has begun a no-confidence vote for the school’s leadership after an alleged gang rape prompted public outcry over sexual assault on college campuses and scrutiny over the university’s handling of the case.

Faculty members started the no-confidence vote on Thursday that is expected to continue until November 6. The initiative is non-binding, but could send a message that president Michael Kotlikoff has lost the confidence of the school’s faculty.

“Hundreds of students, staff, faculty and alumni approached the sponsors of this resolution to emphasize to us that the Jane Doe case is but a tip of the iceberg,” said Paul Ortiz, the lead faculty sponsor of the resolution.

A lawsuit filed last month alleges that a female student, identified as Jane Doe, was drugged and gang raped by seven male students at a fraternity house in 2024.

The case has raised questions about whether the university acted with sufficient urgency or downplayed the alleged abuse in order to protect its reputation. The university initially shut down the fraternity and suspended the male students, two of whom were later expelled.

Faculty considered on Wednesday whether to postpone a vote of no confidence, with some urging patience and others arguing that the vote was a necessary response to institutional reluctance to take the issue seriously.

The Associated Press news agency reported that the debate took place after a group of 20 female science and engineering faculty members called on Kotlikoff to resign in a letter to trustees.

“What our community needed was clear leadership; instead, it faced a leadership vacuum,” the letter stated.

Kotlikoff sought to address the fallout in a statement earlier this month in which he listed a number of preliminary responses.

“I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community,” he said.

Two of the men accused of taking part in the alleged rape of Jane Doe have asked for New York Attorney General Letitia James to be removed from her role overseeing the renewed criminal probe into the case over social media posts from the attorney general expressing support for the accuser prior to her appointment.

A judge on Thursday appeared sceptical of one of the challenges, which James’ office has said are “without merit”.

articles.summary: Jaipur EV registrations top 9,000 in 2026, but owners rely on home charging as public stations are unreliable and highway chargers remain limited.
articles.body: Jaipur: More than 9,000 electric vehicles have been registered in Jaipur in 2026 till now, nearly three times the number recorded in 2023, according to data on the Parivahan Sewa website. However, EV owners said charging infrastructure had failed to keep pace, with several public charging points reportedly non-functional and facilities unreliable for intercity travel.While most owners charge their vehicles at home for daily commutes, unreliable public charging stations and a lack of chargers along highways continue to restrict their use, particularly for longer journeys.Naresh Poswal, an EV owner in Jaipur, said he continues to rely on petrol and diesel-powered vehicles for intercity travel due to lack of charging infrastructure along highways. “If I am planning to go to Kota and return, I have to rely on my petrol or diesel vehicle,” he said.Several EV owners also complained that public charging stations within the city were not always operational at locations near Tripolia Bazaar and Mansarovar.Rinku Pipalawa, another EV owner, said she had attempted to use a charging station on Shipra Path during an emergency but found it non-functional after reaching the location with a low battery. “After that experience, I rarely rely on public charging stations. I make sure my car is sufficiently charged before stepping out, and otherwise use the fuel-powered car I have as an alternative,” she said.Pipalawa too added that she preferred using a petrol or diesel vehicle for long-distance journeys because charging options along highways remained limited.The growing number of EV registrations points to increasing consumer interest in electric mobility. articles.title: No breakthrough in attack on jeweller brothers
articles.summary: Jaipur Jamdoli: Police probe attack on jeweller brothers; no arrests yet despite CCTV review and questioning suspects; robbery angle suspected, 3 injured.
articles.body: Jaipur: A day after two jeweller brothers were attacked with rods and allegedly shot at in Jamdoli, police are yet to identify the assailants despite questioning more than a dozen suspects and examining CCTV footage.Investigators are probing the suspected robbery angle after the attackers allegedly tried to snatch a bag containing jewellery before fleeing with two small jewellery boxes, according to the victims’ family.The victims, Sonu Swarnkar alias Soni (35) and Nishu Soni (38), run S R Jewellers in Radha Govind Vihar. They were returning home on a scooter from their showroom Wednesday night when motorcycle-borne assailants intercepted them about 700 metre from their residence.According to Jamdoli police, the attackers opened fire, causing the brothers to fall off their scooter, then assaulted them with sticks and iron rods when they resisted the attempt to snatch the jewellery bag.Seema Gupta (32), who lives opposite the spot, rushed to help them with stones but was allegedly shot in the leg before the attackers fled.All three injured people were taken to SMS Hospital. Police teams fanned out across nearby areas after the incident and questioned more than 12 suspects, but the identities of the attackers remain unconfirmed. Investigators are examining CCTV footage to trace their movements and establish their identities.Police are also awaiting medical findings to confirm whether Seema sustained pellet injuries. articles.title: Audio recordings reveal decisions made moments before deadly train crash in Spain
articles.summary: What we know about the deadly high-speed train crash in Spain
articles.body: New audio obtained by Spanish media reveals that the operator of a stopped train called a control center to say she could not restart the train as another behind it sped ahead in its direction. The resulting crash of the two high-speed trains Wednesday killed at least 69 people and injured dozens more. As of Thursday, 67 passengers remained missing, according to Spanish officials. Many questions remain about the failures that led to one of Spain’s worst transportation disasters in decades and whether something could have been done to prevent it. Audio recordings of communications between the train operators and staff members at a control center in Madrid shed light on the decisions made in the minutes before the trains collided. Spain’s transportation minister, Óscar Puente, said Wednesday that a security system stopped working because of a computer malfunction, causing multiple trains on the line to stop at about 8:30 a.m. local time. With the computer system down, rail traffic was then handed over to the control center in Madrid. At about 8:36 a.m., the control center authorized a state-owned Renfe high-speed train to resume its journey, without speed limitations, even though a stationary ‌train from the private rail company Iryo was on the tracks ahead, Puente said. An erroneous ​decision was ‌made ⁠to restart the ⁠Renfe train, breaking protocol, he said. Audio obtained by Spanish media of the conversations between the operators of both trains and the control center sheds light on the series of decisions leading up to the collision at about 8:53 a.m., near the train station in Urda. NBC News has not been able to independently verify the authenticity of the audio. After the computer system went down, the control center told the Renfe train operator to resume its journey “at normal speed,” according to an audio clip. “At normal speed? OK,” the operator responded. “OK, we’ll talk later,” the controller said before signing off. Several minutes later, someone from the control center called the Iryo train to authorize it to also continue on its normal journey, according to an audio clip. The operator of the Iryo train, which was ahead of the Renfe train, called back seven minutes later to say she had been unable to restart it. “I’m still stopped at the entrance signal,” she said, according to the audio clip. The control center told her to restart the train when she could and to call back if she had further problems, according to the audio. Several minutes later, the Renfe train ran into the back of the Iryo train. The crash, the second deadly high-speed rail train collision this year in Spain, sent shock waves across the country. Until recently, the high-speed rail network was considered one of Spain’s crowning achievements. The crash came just weeks ahead of a major election in Spain, and it has led to criticism of the government and protests. In January, a separate disaster on the same rail line killed 46 people. Several days later, a commuter train near Barcelona derailed, killing the driver and injuring dozens of other people. Hundreds of emergency workers, firefighters, police officers and soldiers responded to the scene of Wednesday’s crash to rescue survivors and recover bodies. Cranes were brought in to move parts of the damaged trains later in the day. Spain has the largest high-speed rail network in Europe for trains moving at more than 155 mph, with more than 1,900 miles of track, according to the European Union. The identities of victims have begun to emerge. Fátima Báñez, a former minister, was among those killed in the collision, according to the leader of Spain’s opposition Popular Party. “She was a tireless woman, a loyal friend, and always committed to improving the lives of Spaniards,” Alberto Núñez Feijóo wrote in Spanish on social media. Antonio Acedo, the driver of one of the trains, was also killed, according to the Izquierda Española political party. “Antonio was an exceptional person, a kind, prudent, and dedicated man,” the party wrote on social media. The country is observing three days of mourning after the crash. Dirk Llorens, an American who lives in Madrid, said he and his wife were on the stopped train when, suddenly, “I was thrown just violently, just over my table.” “Then the train started sliding, and I could see that the roof had opened, and there was dust flying out of the back,” he said. People were panicking and did not know what had just happened, he said. Llorens thought the train had derailed somehow. He turned and saw that “everything was destroyed.” Llorens said that as he and his wife tried to escape from the train, he saw people who had “smashed their face” during the impact, with bloody noses and cuts on their heads spewing blood. He said that the crash occurred on a hill and that “we were all just trying to get out because we thought the train would roll on the hill and kill us.” As more injured people escaped from the train, Llorens saw a man “come out completely full of blood, and he was just sitting on a tree, just completely collapsed.” “I think people were so in shock. We were all in shock,” he said. Those who were less injured began trying to help one another, he said, adding that soon afterward, a large group of paramedics and police arrived. “You really never know what can happen in life — that makes you appreciate life but also understand that some things can happen at any time,” Llorens said. He called for transparency from the Spanish government about what happened. “The Spanish government really needs to put all their effort in making sure that something like that doesn’t ever happen again,” he said. “I don’t think I’ll take a train in Spain unless I see that they’re having big improvements in what they’re doing.”

articles.title: Kamala Harris breaks with left flank, warns Dems that impeaching Trump is 'not a good idea'
articles.summary: Kamala Harris urged Democrats to focus on investigations and accountability over impeachment, saying the votes aren't there and the party should focus on getting things done.
articles.body: Former Vice President Kamala Harris broke with some on the left flank of the Democratic Party on Wednesday over whether Democrats should pursue impeachment proceedings against President Donald Trump if they regain control of Congress in November. "The Parnas Perspective" host Aaron Parnas asked Harris what she would recommend Congress do if Democrats regain control following the midterm elections. "Would it be to go the investigations route and potentially an impeachment one day," he asked, "or would it be go past policy and force the president to veto it?" JAMES CARVILLE WARNS DEMS AGAINST IMPEACHING TRUMP IF THEY WIN CONTROL IN MIDTERMS "I think that going on in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea. OK, just to be honest with you. Because we have limited resources and I think the energy and the resources need to be put into accountability, need to be put into investigations and that's where the time should be spent. Remember I was in the Senate for the last go-round and the votes aren't there, right? So that's how I feel," Harris said. She argued Democrats need to focus on getting things done and that they should be "ruthless." HOUSE DEMS PLOT TRUMP INVESTIGATION BLITZ IF THEY SEIZE MAJORITY "When I say we should be ruthless, I don't mean cruel, but we should be uncompromising and not sit around, you know, being genteel about the relationships and instead actually get stuff done, whether it be about accountability or restoring, for example, what they took in terms of the Medicaid cuts, restoring what we need to do around some check and balance around this war nobody wants," the former VP said. Some Democrats in Congress have pushed again to impeach Trump, who was impeached twice during his first term in office but acquitted in the Senate on both occasions. Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, forced a vote on a resolution to impeach Trump over his administration's immigration enforcement policies, including the deaths of people during federal immigration operations earlier this year. The move divided House Democrats, whose leaders have largely avoided emphasizing impeachment as they work to regain control of Congress in the November midterms. Florida Democratic Senate candidate and state Rep. Angie Nixon said in an interview with Politico that she would not oppose impeachment hearings and would vote to remove Trump if elected. "The Daily Show" host Jon Stewart expressed a similar sentiment during a question-and-answer segment at the end of his "The Weekly Show" podcast. He was asked whether Democrats should seek to impeach Trump if they regain control of Congress in the midterm elections. REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: DEMOCRATS FACE AN IMPEACHMENT TRACTOR BEAM THAT COULD DERAIL THEIR AFFORDABILITY MESSAGE He said he wanted Democrats to make a full-scale effort to rebalance the economy rather than hold performative hearings. "I don't want to see a f---ing five-act performative play of House hearings," Stewart said. "I just don't want to see it. I don't want to see everybody having the opportunity to pantomime accountability because you know they're actually not going to bring it." "There will be enormous pressure to seek accountability if Democrats win control in either or both chambers next week, but the push to make things better for the American people may be even more intense. If successful, Democrats would be wise to try to strike some balance and to work on parallel tracks to deliver results. Voters want justice and accountability, but they want affordable gas and groceries more," Costas Panagopoulos, a professor of political science at Northeastern University, told Fox News Digital of Harris' remarks. Republican strategist Liz Mair, head of Mair strategies, said Harris was "right," in a statement to Fox News Digital. She added, "Democrats will win these midterms not because swing voters who deliver those victories want them to spend the next two years impeaching the president, but because they want them to focus on bringing costs down or at least limiting ongoing price hikes." DEM MAKING SENATE COMEBACK BID SAYS HE WOULDN'T SUPPORT A TRUMP IMPEACHMENT PUSH "Every second Democrats spend trying to impeach President Trump again is a minute they're not spending addressing affordability challenges, and appeasing their base at the expense of doing what they will literally have been elected to accomplish," Mair said. Harris has endorsed several big institutional changes, such as Supreme Court expansion, possibly getting rid of the Electoral College, and Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico statehood. articles.title: Israel election result shows no overall majority as vote count complete
articles.summary: Opposition explores options to form coalition as no party secures the 61 seats required for parliamentary majority.
articles.body:
Vote counting is complete in Israel’s elections with neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition winning a majority in parliament, Israeli media have said.

As the provisional results were being published on Thursday, opposition politicians met to explore options for a coalition.

With more than 99 percent of Tuesday’s ballots tallied, Netanyahu’s bloc held 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset while the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot secured 48 seats, Israeli outlet Haaretz reported. The Arab list parties, meanwhile, held a combined 19 seats, it added.

Both Netanyahu’s bloc and the opposition parties fell short of securing the 61 seats required for a parliamentary majority.

The final results of the Knesset elections will be certified and announced by Wednesday. Until that date, the results are subject to change.

Tuesday’s elections – the first since the October 7, 2023, attacks on southern Israel and the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza – were widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s premiership.

On Thursday, Eisenkot, who heads the Yashar party, met former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, who leads the Together party, to discuss ways to form a new government “as quickly as possible”, according to a statement reported by Israel’s Ynet News outlet.

Eisenkot also met Democrats party chairman Yair Golan, the only member of the opposition alliance to support forming a coalition with parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel, while all other political groups have rejected any such union.

Golan met separately with Mansour Abbas, who leads the United Arab list, or Ra’am, which is projected to win seven of the 19 Arab party seats.

“This is a time for action. Our responsibility is not to miss the opportunity for change and the salvation of Israel,” Golan said in a post on X after his meeting with Abbas.

Al Jazeera correspondent Nour Odeh noted that “Eisenkot has an uphill battle ahead of him.”

The former military leader-turned-politician has pledged “not to ally himself or get into a partnership with the Palestinian Israeli parties”, Odeh said, reporting from the occupied West Bank because Al Jazeera is banned from Israel.

But given the fact that no political bloc has a majority, the Eisenkot-led opposition bloc cannot form a governing coalition without the support of Arab-led parties, she added.

Netanyahu ‘using state institutions for his personal needs’

Meanwhile, Netanyahu’s Likud party has continued to amplify unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, potentially with foreign assistance – claims that have been rejected .

The head of the Central Elections Committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, said “serious suspicions” of foreign interference had been brought to him in a letter to the Shin Bet security agency. Sohlberg said he could not verify the claims, but given their serious nature, he asked the agency to investigate.

Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of working to delegitimise the election results with his allegations.

In a video posted on his X account, Eisenkot said: “The days of Netanyahu using state institutions against Israeli interests for his personal needs are over,” adding that no “spin” can change voters rejecting his government at the polls.

“Benjamin Netanyahu is not satisfied with the results, no matter how much he has been saying that he won,” political analyst Xavier Abu Eid told Al Jazeera.

He added that while it seems unlikely the opposition could take advantage by overcoming differences with the Arab-led groups, there could be an understanding to replace the current speaker of the Knesset, who is close to Netanyahu.

“If there is a new speaker in the Knesset, … Netanyahu loses an important ally,” Abu Eid said, adding that this might give an opening for the opposition to “actually start passing legislation” against him.

Odeh said the next steps would involve negotiations between political groups after the Central Elections Committee announces and certifies the election results by Wednesday.

articles.title: Canada seeks EU ‘associate member’ status as Carney counters Trump’s trade pressure
articles.summary: Canadian prime minister Mark Carney and European commission president Ursula von der Leyen on Thursday pressed for a closer alliance between Canada and
articles.body: Canadian prime minister Mark Carney and European commission president Ursula von der Leyen on Thursday pressed for a closer alliance between Canada and the European Union, pitching it as a way to protect their economic sovereignty amid US president Donald Trump’s trade war and mounting pressure on traditional allies.The proposed partnership could make Canada the EU’s first “associate member”, bringing it closer to the bloc without formal membership. The two leaders also backed a broader “Alliance for the Future”, envisaged as a framework for cooperation on trade, defence, critical minerals, technology and research.“When trade becomes a tool of economic pressure, it is families that pay the price, from the supermarket shelf to the cost of a new car,” von der Leyen said in Montreal. “We are seeing in real time our sovereignty being attacked.”Von der Leyen warned that economic ties once seen as a source of stability were increasingly being used as instruments of coercion, particularly where countries depended on single suppliers for energy, semiconductors and critical minerals.Carney said a deeper partnership would help Canada absorb economic shocks and resist attempts by foreign governments and powerful technology companies to dictate its choices.“Why does sovereignty matter in a dangerous and divided world? It allows us to withstand shocks,” he said. “It allows us to live our lives as we choose.”The push comes as Trump has suggested that Canada’s proposed arrangement with the EU could amount to a “hostile act” and threatened tariffs on Europe if he deemed the move unfriendly. A senior Canadian government official said Wednesday that closer ties with Europe were not directed against the US but reflected longstanding shared interests.Carney sought to play down the debate over the proposed associate-member label, saying the substance of the partnership mattered more than its name. “This new alliance is not a marketing exercise. The name doesn’t matter,” he said.He later used the term “associate member” himself at a business roundtable with von der Leyen, highlighting the potential benefits for Canadian businesses, researchers and consumers. Carney has ruled out full EU membership and said any enhanced partnership would require a vote in Canada’s Parliament.Associate-member proposal faces resistanceVon der Leyen showed no sign of abandoning the proposal, despite concerns among some EU member states. Canada cannot join the bloc as a full member because of geography, she said, but both sides wanted to take their relationship to the “highest level possible”.“This is why we are discussing the idea of Canada becoming the first associate member of the European Union,” she said, describing the proposed arrangement as an “association without accession”.The model could bring Canada closer to the EU than any previous arrangement with a country outside the bloc, with deeper cooperation on artificial intelligence, energy, defence and other sectors.Anand Sundar, a special adviser at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said France and Germany were among the countries unhappy with the designation and that it might not survive the summit.“The fact that member states have rejected the associate membership framing is very embarrassing for von der Leyen,” Sundar said.The two-day summit, also attended by European Council President Antonio Costa, is expected to launch the broader “Alliance for the Future”. Von der Leyen said other like-minded, trusted countries would be welcome to join that initiative, which is distinct from the more ambitious associate-member proposal.She said Canada and the EU would finalise an agreement on Friday to give Canadian companies, startups and researchers access to Europe’s network of 12 advanced supercomputers, strengthening cooperation on artificial intelligence. The sides also plan to improve strategic supply chains and encourage joint investment in industries considered critical to economic security, with officials hoping the wider partnership could be endorsed in 2027.Trade and defence ties in focusCanada already has significant economic links with the EU through the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), which eliminated most tariffs. It is also the only non-European country participating in the EU’s 150-billion-euro ($167-billion) SAFE defence procurement programme, which allows Canadian companies to participate in joint European military purchases.Further defence cooperation, however, faces competing priorities within the bloc. Sundar said France was pushing for strict “Made in Europe” rules that could restrict Canadian firms’ access to future EU defence spending, while Germany favoured broader participation.Critical minerals are another area of potential cooperation as both sides seek to diversify supply chains. Von der Leyen said the value of EU imports of Canadian critical raw materials rose 62% last year to 3.3 billion euros ($3.7 billion), including lithium, cobalt, nickel and graphite.The US accounted for 71.7% of Canada’s merchandise exports in 2025. Carney has set a goal of doubling exports to other countries over the next decade, reducing Canada’s reliance on its southern neighbour.Carney’s push for closer ties with Europe builds on a warning he delivered at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, when he said the US-led international order was breaking down and urged middle powers to unite against economic coercion by major powers.You use AI every day. articles.title: A university in Cyprus launched a free blockchain course in 2014; its online programme has attracted more than 150,000 learners from over 120 countries
articles.summary: Free online blockchain course from the University of Nicosia in Cyprus has drawn more than 150,000 learners from over 120 countries since its launch in
articles.body: Free online blockchain course from the University of Nicosia in Cyprus has drawn more than 150,000 learners from over 120 countries since its launch in 2014. The university describes the programme on blockchain and digital assets as the first course of its kind at any university, and says it is one of the largest university-led blockchain learning initiatives in the world. Its autumn 2026 edition began on 28 September, combining free teaching with an advanced paid track, hardware wallet rewards and scholarships. For those curious about Bitcoin and digital money, it shows how one course can become a global classroom.Professor George Giaglis says the course began because no university taught Bitcoin properlyGeorge Giaglis, Executive Director of the Institute for the Future at the University of Nicosia, said in an announcement from the university that the course was created because there was nowhere in the university system to learn about Bitcoin properly. Twelve years on, he said, the subject has a regulatory regime, an institutional market and a serious research literature, and the curriculum has had to keep pace with all three. What has not changed, he added, is that “the first eight weeks are free to anyone with an internet connection”, and he said they always will be.\A free eight-week introductory track sits alongside a paid advanced track that costs €199The introductory track covers weeks one to eight and costs nothing. It includes the full curriculum on blockchain foundations, Bitcoin and digital money, Ethereum and programmable blockchains, wallet security and privacy, decentralised finance, prediction markets, the geopolitics of cryptocurrency, and tokenisation and stablecoins. Students also receive weekly quizzes, live question-and-answer sessions, a final exam, a certificate of completion and access to a global student community.The advanced track covers weeks nine to twelve and costs €199. It adds four weeks on non-fungible tokens and digital ownership, the regulation and policy of digital assets, blockchain scaling and design trade-offs, and the convergence of blockchain with artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things. Advanced students also get a blockchain-verifiable certificate, extended access to course materials, dedicated networking channels and daily cryptocurrency market briefings. Anyone already registered for the introductory track can upgrade.Hardware wallets, sponsorships and scholarships reward students who complete the courseAccording to the University of Nicosia, the autumn edition comes with 1,000 hardware wallets and €37,000 in scholarships. Students who pass the introductory final exam enter a draw for 50 Trezor Model T hardware wallets, drawn on a blockchain from the pool of successful candidates. Every student who completes the advanced track receives a Trezor Model T wallet. Cardano is sponsoring 25 advanced-track places, each valued at €199, and Ripple is backing five scholarships towards the university’s Master of Science in Blockchain and Digital Currency, each valued at €7,400.Faculty and industry guests from Ripple, Cardano, Trezor and Avalanche shape the autumn teachingUniversity faculty teach the course, including Dr Apostolos Kourtis and Dr Lambis Dionysopoulos alongside Giaglis, with contributions from industry experts Garrick Hileman, Jeff Bandman and Punk6529. The autumn edition adds guest sessions from John Greene, technical writer at the Cardano Foundation; Patrick Tobler, co-founder of Masumi Network and founder and chief executive officer of NMKR; Brandon M. Procak, director of stablecoin strategy and operations at Ripple; Lucien Bourdon, Bitcoin analyst at Trezor; and Luke Martinez, head of global operations at Team1 (Avalanche). The curriculum, assessment and certification remain under the university’s academic direction.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Bukele adds a wildcard to Haiti’s fractured security landscape
articles.summary: What could go wrong? For over a week, El Salvador has been quietly sending troops to Haiti, a project whose scale was only revealed publicly last night: More than 2,000 Salvadoran soldiers will be sent to the Caribbean nation, but their mission and mandate remain opaque.
articles.body: What could go wrong? For over a week, El Salvador has been quietly sending troops to Haiti, a project whose scale was only revealed publicly last night: More than 2,000 Salvadoran soldiers will be sent to the Caribbean nation, but their mission and mandate remain opaque. The deployment is a wildcard in Port-au-Prince, a city of densely-inhabited hills where battle lines constantly shift between dozens of gangs and anti-gang groups, including foreign forces, neighborhood vigilantes, and mercenaries. Two thousand soldiers is a significant arrival here. That’s more than Haiti’s entire army, and about a quarter of the urban footprint of the Haitian National Police. It’s about equal to the current staffing of the multinational UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) and far outnumbers the private military contractors on the Haitian government’s secretive “task force.” But how do they fit into Haiti’s fractured security landscape? Who is paying for it all? And what exactly is their mission? For now, the Salvadoran forces’ command structure has not been established, according to a source close to the matter. Little light was shed by parallel communiqués released Wednesday evening by El Salvador and Haiti, which described a call between President Nayib Bukele and interim Haitian leader Alix Didier Fils-Aimé about the overall security situation and status of four missing Salvadorans air technicians. The air technicians, catalyst for this deployment, disappeared earlier this month after an apparent gang ambush. They had been working with the GSF in a noncombat role, according to Salvadoran officials. In the immediate aftermath, 100 Salvadoran special forces were sent to Haiti to assist in search and rescue operations — a precursor to the now expanded force. Ten days later, local sources say it is unlikely that the missing four can be recovered. If Salvadoran forces cannot achieve that, they’ll likely seek other wins, perhaps joining one of several existing security forces for an extended push against the gangs in retaliation. A clue to their plans may eventually lie with their physical location; at time of reporting, the Salvadorans were not staying at the main GSF base. Bukele has argued that he has unique bona fides to address Haiti’s crisis. His government’s own hardline crackdown on gangs back home did restore peace to what was once the most violent country in the Western Hemisphere — though critics highlight his use of mass incarceration and accusations of widespread abuses. In a message posted to X last week, he addressed the gangs in Haitian Creole: “There is still time to avoid this,” Bukele said. “Return our four countrymen to us alive and unharmed and everything will return to the way it was before the kidnapping.” Most residents of Port-au-Prince would rather see dramatic change, after years of brutal gang violence that have driven over a million people from their homes. Just two hours from Florida’s coast, the city is terrorized by frequent gang kidnappings, rape and arson, all broadcast on social media. On Thursday, Haitians nationwide were reminded again of just how much insecurity has put civil life on pause, with the news that long-deferred presidential elections are postponed yet again until next year. But experts warn about the dangers of additional players on a crowded urban battlefield. “The situation is volatile and could become more violent with innocent people being harmed,” Bill O’Neill, the UN’s human rights expert for Haiti, said. Romain LeCoeur, Haiti expert at the Global Initiative against Transnational Organized Crime, echoed the concern. “Haiti’s security response no longer rests on a single strategy, but on a juxtaposition of multilateral, national and private actors, each operating under its own rules,” he said. “As long as no one can say who decides and who is accountable, every operation risks adding to the confusion rather than to security.” Reporting contributed by CNN’s Merlin Delcid in El Salvador.

articles.title: Stormy weather could hit key states on Election Day, forecasters predict
articles.summary: A line of thunderstorms could stretch from Texas to Missouri on Tuesday, with rain in Iowa and strong winds in Kansas.
articles.body: Stormy, wet weather is expected to hammer the central U.S. on Election Day, with the spiciest forecasts for states with some of the hottest races — including Texas, Kansas and Iowa. Forecasters predict a line of thunderstorms stretching from Texas to Missouri on Tuesday, with dreary rainfall in upper Midwest states like Iowa and strong winds in Plains states like Kansas. With attention focused on voter turnout in battleground states, the inclement weather could affect candidates’ ability to draw people to the polls. “The middle part of the country is going to be probably the most active area on Election Day,” said Bob Oravec, a lead forecaster at the National Weather Service’s Weather Prediction Center. “Depending on how committed people are going to be to turning out for whatever candidate they’re going to vote for, the weather could have an impact.” Oravec said forecasting models for Tuesday morning show thunderstorms hammering north-central Texas, a critical battleground in the state’s U.S. Senate race, in which Democrat James Talarico faces Republican Ken Paxton. “The usual things of severe weather” were all possibilities, he said: “high winds, large hail, maybe even tornadoes.” Although Tuesday is more than five days away, Oravec said the National Weather Service is confident that a storm system will sweep across the West Coast on Sunday then hit the central states Tuesday. “This is the kind of system that our numerical models handle well,” he said. “The individual timing of a line of thunderstorms likely will change over the next few days. But the overall idea of the storm moving from west to east is pretty well set.” Other areas in the central U.S. could face hazards, too. The Weather Prediction Center forecasts high winds in the Plains states, including in Kansas, Colorado and Nebraska. “We’re looking at sustained winds around 20 to 30 miles an hour, and we could see some gusts over 40 to maybe even over 50 miles an hour,” said Clint Alexander, a National Weather Service forecaster in Goodland, Kansas. Alexander said the winds could affect travel, including on Interstate 70, the main east-west corridor through the state, though the forecast remains somewhat uncertain. Kansas has become a surprise battleground for the U.S. Senate, with polls showing Republican Sen. Roger Marshall and Democrat Adam Hamilton neck and neck. Iowa, meanwhile, has close races brewing for governor and U.S. Senate. Conditions there on Tuesday may be extremely wet. “It’ll be pretty dreary,” said Justin Schultz, the lead forecaster for the National Weather Service in Davenport, Iowa. “There looks to be a good bit of rainfall falling right on Election Day for at least portions of the state.” Schultz expects the forecast for Iowa to firm up over the weekend. There’s no flooding predicted, but his team thinks a measurement called precipitable water — the amount of moisture present in a column of the atmosphere — could reach an all-time high. That would amount to a lot of rain and wet conditions throughout the day. “It could actually be near-record moisture for this time of the year,” Schultz said.

articles.title: Hyrox athlete who soiled herself in race admits putting others at risk but says backlash was traumatic
articles.summary: In her first interview since the incident, Joanna Wietrzyk told the BBC she takes responsibility for it but did not deserve such a severe backlash.
articles.body:
An Australian athlete has admitted putting others at risk by continuing to race after soiling herself during an endurance sports event.

Speaking exclusively to the BBC ahead of her return to the sport, Joanna Wietrzyk suggested her determination to win the Hyrox race in Beijing in September had clouded her judgement: "It was my decision to continue racing so I take full responsibility for that."

Challenged over why she carried on, she said: "I didn't really think about those around me… the decision that I made in hindsight was the wrong decision and I'm truly sorry for everyone that I did affect."

The 24-year-old said that the experience and subsequent backlash was "traumatic". She also said she had considered walking away from the sport, in which she holds a world record.

Roughly halfway through her event, Wietrzyk suffered a bout of diarrhoea. Images of faecal matter on parts of her body were then shared widely online.

Asked whether officials should have stopped her, she said no-one encouraged her to do so the time.

Hyrox's co-founder, Moritz Fürste, has issued an apology saying it had been a mistake not to react immediately during the race.

New rules have now been introduced giving race directors the power to remove athletes if their vomit, urine or faeces pose a risk of contamination or threaten the welfare of themselves or others in a race that is primarily held indoors using shared equipment.

Hyrox sees participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises, including a sled push, burpee jumps, indoor rowing, and lunges while carrying a sandbag.

The competition has exploded in popularity since it was founded in 2017 in Hamburg, in northern Germany, and is now held across the world.

Although initially defiant in a now-deleted Instagram post, Wietrzyk apologised in the week after the Beijing event and said she would forfeit the win and retroactively withdraw from the race.

Due to compete in Hamburg on Friday, she said she was "nervous" about her return and hoped that the high-profile incident would not define her.

"I don't want it to become my identity," she said.

In her first interview since Beijing, Wietrzyk said she had suffered a bacterial infection from food poisoning but had gone into the race "feeling fresh, feeling really, really good".

"It was a very sudden experience," she told the BBC.

"It wasn't until about halfway through the race where everything did transpire... In that moment, right then and there, as a very competitive person… and an elite athlete that I am, my only focus is on racing.

"I didn't really think about those around me which, looking back and looking back at the decision that I made, in hindsight, was the wrong decision and I'm truly sorry for everyone that I did affect in that situation."

Following the incident, some of Wietrzyk's co-competitors at September's tournament in Beijing demanded an apology from Hyrox.

Hyrox China has since reportedly refunded some competitors their entry fees.

Wietrzyk admitted that: "Obviously I did put other people at risk."

She also said she regretted an initial social media post published after the race which included the words "Go hard or go home" and "a win is a win". She said she had been in "flight or fight mode" as she sought hospital treatment.

"I didn't really account for what the public would have seen that situation as."

Challenged over whether her apology could be seen as an effort at damage limitation, or too late, she said that she hadn't expected so much exposure from the incident.

"I needed those days to reflect on it and process it."

Speaking about the mentality of elite athletes, she said: "They're so hyper-vigilant on winning and doing the best that they can, putting their training to good use and showcasing their fitness to the world."

After reflecting over the past weeks, she said: "There is more to life… than just racing and just winning."

After Wietrzyk's identity was shared online, Hyrox said anyone sending abuse or threats to the athlete would be banned from future events.

Wietrzyk told the BBC that it had been a "mentally and emotionally taxing period" and she had not expected the global scrutiny, saying her family had also received threats.

The backlash, "Was very eye-opening for me to see the effect of social media nowadays especially from someone who's 24, just out there racing.

"Yes, I did make the wrong decision but I don't believe I should have received such backlash and such scrutiny online … At the end of the day I'm only human."

Wietrzyk said that she had been mainly offline and sought to "isolate herself from the world" for a time but, "I can't do that forever."

"I still have so much more I can achieve in this sport so I think, for me, my mental resilience is the key here where I can inspire others through what I've been through."

articles.title: Israel tightens airline security after flydubai hijacking
articles.summary: Israel has tightened security requirements for airlines operating flights to and from the country, requiring carriers to submit crew details 48 hours
articles.body: Israel has tightened security requirements for airlines operating flights to and from the country, requiring carriers to submit crew details 48 hours before departure, a month after an attempted hijacking of a flydubai flight exposed gaps in the screening of foreign pilots and airline personnel.The new directives, issued Thursday by Israel’s National Center for Passenger Data Analysis, apply to all incoming and outgoing flights operated by Israeli and foreign airlines. Carriers must provide crew information at least 48 hours before departure, submit any subsequent updates no later than two hours before takeoff and issue a final list at takeoff, according to The Times of Israel.The measures were ordered by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu following a security review and are intended to give authorities sufficient time to conduct background checks, Bloomberg reported.The changes follow an incident on September 30, when Omani copilot Hamam al-Hammami allegedly attacked Captain Smit Machchhar, the Indian pilot commanding a Flydubai flight carrying Israeli passengers from Dubai to Tel Aviv, and attempted to seize control of the aircraft. Despite being seriously injured, Machchhar managed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew members to intervene and overpower the attacker. Two off-duty Flydubai pilots who were travelling on the flight subsequently took over the controls and diverted the damaged aircraft to Tabuk in Saudi Arabia, where it landed safely.Machchhar and fellow flydubai crew members were recently honoured by the UAE with the First Class Order of Zayed II for their actions during the incident. The award was conferred by UAE president Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, with the medals presented by Dubai Crown Prince Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum.The incident raised questions about how Hammami had been cleared to operate the route, particularly after reports that he had previously been grounded by Oman Air after extremist material was found in his possession.New screening measuresIsrael’s Channel 13 reported that non-Israeli pilots, cabin crew and passengers travelling to or from the country will also be required to complete an online form 48 hours before entry. The forms will be reviewed by the Population Authority, while people arriving from countries designated as “red” will face additional scrutiny of entry forms and visa applications by the Mossad and Shin Bet, the report said.The Shin Bet, which previously oversaw security relating to Israeli airlines and provided security arrangements for flights departing Israel, will now also be responsible for procedures governing incoming foreign airlines and their overseas departure points.The changes follow reports of longstanding shortcomings in Israel’s oversight of foreign aviation security. According to Channel 13, airlines had been submitting crew lists shortly before departure, in some cases as late as 15 minutes after takeoff, leaving authorities little time to identify potential risks.A separate report cited an internal National Security Council document indicating that the Transportation Ministry had failed to fulfil responsibilities assigned to it for foreign airline security. The ministry had reportedly warned that it lacked the resources and operational capacity to carry out the duties, while an earlier warning in March 2025 flagged failures to comply with a cabinet directive on aviation security.The controversy also centred on access to passenger and crew data. Although the transportation ministry was authorised to access the National Center for Passenger Data Analysis’s database for aviation security purposes, reports said it had not taken the necessary steps to establish that access.Kan News reported that more than 1,200 crew members from countries without diplomatic relations with Israel, including Oman, Syria and Lebanon, had entered the country since the beginning of 2026. The figure has not been independently verified in the reports provided.The new rules are intended to close gaps in the screening process by giving Israeli authorities more time to examine crew information before flights depart.You use AI every day.
